# OpenAI Disrupted Two AI Disinformation Operations. Here's What That Means for You.

> **In short:** OpenAI says it shut down two influence operations that used AI to pose as journalists and run a think tank to spread geopolitical messages. The case shows how AI is making coordinated disinformation faster and more believable — and why every reader needs a sharper eye.

You probably saw a news link this week that looked legitimate. Maybe a "reporter" on a small outlet shared a sharp take on a current conflict. Maybe a "policy expert" at a "think tank" was quoted on something you already felt strongly about. Maybe you didn't think twice about it.

That's exactly the kind of work OpenAI says it just disrupted.

## What OpenAI says it found

According to OpenAI's announcement, the company identified and took down two **influence operations** — coordinated campaigns designed to shape what people think about world events. What made these different was the use of AI to build the **false fronts** (fake online identities and organizations that look real at first glance) the campaigns relied on.

One operation posed as a network of journalists. It created the kind of articles, profiles, and online outlets that, at a glance, look like a small but real newsroom.

The other set up a **think tank** — a research-style organization that publishes reports and commentary to influence policy debates. According to OpenAI, the think tank wasn't real; it was a false front the operation used to look legitimate.

Both operations pushed **geopolitical messaging** — content designed to shape opinions about international affairs.

## Why AI makes this different

Coordinated disinformation isn't new. What's changed is the cost. AI lets a small group produce in a day what used to take a team of writers, researchers, and designers weeks. It can write in many languages, generate profile pictures for fake "staff," and build plausible-looking websites.

The result is more volume, more polish, and a lower chance that any single piece will trip your suspicion.

## What this means for you

- **If you read the news online**: Before you trust a story, look up the outlet. Is there an "About" page with real names? Can you find those journalists elsewhere? A two-minute check beats a strong reaction.
- **If a "study" or "expert" is cited**: Search the expert's name. Real researchers have a trail — past papers, university pages, conference talks. A blank page is a red flag.
- **If the content makes you feel a strong emotion quickly**: That's not always bad journalism, but it's a reason to slow down. Coordinated campaigns are designed to spark exactly that reaction.
- **For business owners and communicators**: Watch for fake accounts that imitate your brand or industry. The same playbook used against the public can be used against companies.

## Wrap-up

OpenAI disrupting two operations doesn't end the problem — it spotlights it. As AI gets cheaper and easier to use, these campaigns will keep coming. The good news is that a few small habits — checking who is actually behind what you read, searching for the experts cited, pausing on emotionally charged stories — go a long way. Pick one news story you saw this week and run one of those checks on it. You'll be doing more media literacy than most people do in a year.
